newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK dlr debt paper holds firm as handover nears.
newsitem.headline: HK dlr debt paper holds firm as handover nears.

text.p: The market for Hong Kong dollar-denominated debt maintained its firm tone amid quiet activity on the last trading day before Hong Kong's handover to China, traders said on Friday.
Traders' minds were more on the holidays and handover celebration parties than on debt issues, traders noted.
"Anything that needed to be done was done one or two weeks ago," a trader at a European bank said.
Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
Markets will be closed on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesay next week to mark the historic occassion.

Traders said spreads on Hong Kong dollar-denominated paper with remaining lives of three to five years have narrowed by three to five basis points over the past six weeks as investors gave Hong Kong a vote of confidence.
Rating agency Standard and Poor's Corp raised Hong Kong's local currency debt rating to AA-minus from A-plus in May.
It raised the territory's foreign currency rating to A-plus from Single-A and at the same time, upgraded China's foreign currency debt rating to BBB-plus from BBB.

Traders said Bank of China's HK$4 billion floating rate certificate of deposit due in September 2001 was trading at 37-38 basis points over the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate on Friday, compared with 40 basis points a month ago.
Chase Manhattan Bank's three-year Hong Kong dollar issue launched in mid-June has tightened by two basis points to trade at 22/23 basis points over HIBOR, traders said.
Hongkong and Shanghai Bank's three-year paper paid 27 basis points to the syndicate when it was launched in early May and has consolidated at 25/26 basis points, they said.
The paper had tightened to 23 basis points after S&P raised HSBC's long-term credit rating to A-plus from Single-A in tandem with its upgrade of Hong Kong.
Traders said a growing number of international banks are willing to take Hong Kong dollar debt issues, reversing a more cautious attitude of one or two years ago.

Two years ago, the outlook for Hong Kong dollar debt was seen as "uncertain" because of political risk associated with the handover and as restrictive economic policies in China dampened growth, a trader at a Japanese bank said.
